newsitem.title: CUBA: Japan envoy in Cuba for talks on Lima crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan envoy in Cuba for talks on Lima crisis.

text.p: Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura arrived in Havana on Wednesday for talks with President Fidel Castro on Cuba's possible help in ending a hostage crisis in Peru now into its fourth month.
Komura, who flew to the Cuban capital after a two-day trip to Lima, was due to meet Castro later on Wednesday, Cuban officials said.

Japanese diplomatic sources said in Lima that Komura sought to formalise a request from Tokyo that Cuba grant asylum to Peru's Marxist rebel hostage-takers if a negotiated solution to the 92-day crisis is reached. The rebels are holding 72 people captive at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
Komura, met by Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Jorge Bolanos, spoke only briefly to reporters at Havana airport and did not comment on the purpose of his 24-hour trip.
Castro told Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori in Havana earlier this month that Cuba was willing to grant asylum to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers.
The Cuban leader, calling such an offer a "moral duty," said at the time that all parties involved, including the rebels, would have to agree formally to such a move.
Following Fujimori's trip to Havana, the rebels told reporters they wanted to stay in Peru but said they reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.
Komura arrived from two days in Lima cautioning Peru's government against using force to end the siege and pressing for a speedy settlement to the crisis.
"I have met with Fujimori and I hope there will be progress towards a peaceful solution of this incident," Komura told reporters in Havana.

He said the guarantors' commission, a three-man mediation panel made up of representatives from the Red Cross, Canada and the Vatican, would help "make the conversations a little more agile." Komura added he hoped the Peruvian government would respond to these efforts by the commision.
Talks between the Peruvian authorities and the hostage-takers are stalled over the MRTA's main demand for the release of some 450 jailed comrades.

Komura was to travel on Thurday afternoon to the Dominican Republic, which like Cuba has offered asylum for some of the MRTA members. Despite the diplomatic moves, the MRTA has given no indication it will accept asylum or end its siege with anything less than the release of its jailed members.

Fujimori has rejected that demand, but he is believed to be considering concessions such as improving harsh jail conditions for rebels convicted of terrorism or releasing a small number of MRTA rebels not yet sentenced or convicted on lesser charges.
Cuba played a cautious role in the affair from the start. While the MRTA are said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution, Havana for weeks declined comment on the affair.

Castro's government waited to be asked by Fujimori before offering possible asylum to the rebels, and insisted at that time that all parties involved would have to be in formal agreement if such a move took place.
Bolanos said on Wednesday that Cuba's position on the issue had not changed.
If the rebels do come to the communist-ruled island, there will be precedents.
Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure the freedom of the brother of former Colombian President Cesar Gaviria. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota.
Former M-19 guerrilla Rosemberg Pabon, who led the assault on the Dominican Embassy, said dialogue was the only one way out.
"Let's talk! Let's talk! What is needed is a climate of dialogue," Pabon told a seminar on the Lima crisis.
